articles.title: New study explores how money influences interpretations of the Bible
articles.summary: A large survey of Americans reveals that household income strongly shapes how religious individuals interpret the Bible’s teachings on charity, challenging the long-held idea that faith universally suppresses the desire for systemic economic change.

articles.title: Diets high in fat and sugar are linked to impulsiveness in people with borderline personality disorder
articles.summary: Adults with borderline personality disorder who ate more foods high in fat and sugar tended to be more impulsive and took more risks on a gambling task, though their diets were unrelated to overall symptom severity.

articles.title: A mirror trick that adds a sixth finger also changes what people think their hand can grab
articles.summary: With a mirror and some well-timed brushstrokes, researchers gave volunteers the sensation of a sixth finger. Afterward, people judged that their hand needed a wider opening to fit through and could grasp larger blocks.

articles.title: Intelligence and fertility: Do smarter people have fewer children? The strongest evidence suggests a smaller, more complicated link
articles.summary: People with higher intelligence scores tend to have slightly smaller families in American and British surveys. But when researchers wait until people finish having children and compare brothers from the same families, the link shrinks or even reverses.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
articles.summary: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

articles.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
articles.summary: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.

articles.title: A strong emotional bond with a mother predicts resilience after childhood trauma
articles.summary: A large study reveals that adolescents who experience a warm relationship with a mother figure and limit their sedentary screen time are more likely to demonstrate resilience in adulthood following childhood abuse.

articles.title: Men and women report similar levels of “duty sex,” and similar reasons behind it
articles.summary: Sex out of obligation is often treated as a red flag in relationships. But a new study suggests it may serve a purpose for some people, appearing most often when they sense their relationship could be under threat.

articles.title: Horror isn’t just intense fear, new psychology study suggests
articles.summary: Fear tends to involve possible danger ahead, while horror often follows learning about something that shouldn’t happen. A new study suggests that graphic, extreme descriptions of harm push readers toward horror by making events feel abnormal.

articles.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
articles.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.
